lines.text: A flight simulator can be fast on average and still fail its pilot. All it takes is one late answer.
lines.source: old lab film, line 0: fast on average, can one late response break the budget

lines.text: When the pilot moves the controls, the simulator has to answer in about the time of a blink. That limit is a rule, not a goal. Miss it, and the hours flown do not count.
lines.source: old lab film, lines 1 and 3: transport delay is a regulated ceiling (150 ms, FAA Part 60 / EASA CS-FSTD(A)); a blink lasts roughly 100 to 400 ms; a device over the ceiling does not qualify

lines.text: Every stage spends part of that time, from the controls to the motion of the cabin. Drawing the world takes the largest share.
lines.source: old lab film, line 2: every stage spends the budget, image generation the largest share (illustrative stage budget)

lines.text: And Europe's newest standard tightens the limit for the most realistic new simulators. A chain that passed before would now fail.
lines.source: old lab film, line 4: EASA CS-FSTD Issue 1 (ED Decision 2026/008/R, p. 467) sets 100 ms at fidelity level S for new devices

lines.text: Inside, the simulator runs on a beat, many times a second. A late frame is late, however fast the frames around it were.
lines.source: old lab film, lines 5 and 6: a fixed cadence (60 Hz); a deadline is never met on average

lines.text: A training session is a long run of frames. Even a failure that looks vanishingly rare comes back again and again, and the pilot feels every one.
lines.source: old lab film, lines 7 and 8: count the frames; a four-hour session at 60 Hz is 864,000 frames, and one in a thousand is 864 stutters

lines.text: And failures don't spread out politely. They arrive in bursts, so the real thing is worse.
lines.source: old lab film, line 9: independence is the optimistic case; real overruns cluster

lines.text: A simulator is not one computer. It is a rack of them, all feeding the same frame, and the frame is only done when the last one reports.
lines.source: old lab film, lines 10 and 11: a rack of hosts publishes into one frame; the frame ends with the last host, latency is a maximum

lines.text: So one slow computer makes the frame late for everyone. An average across the rack hides it. Each computer needs its own budget, enforced.
lines.source: old lab film, lines 13 and 14: one straggler makes the frame late; budgets are allocated and enforced per host, a system average constrains nobody

lines.text: None of it counts unless it is measured while the session runs. Count every overrun. A spike can hide between two samples.
lines.source: old lab film, lines 15 to 17: instrument while the session runs; trust the overrun counter, sampled step time misses spikes

lines.text: Determinism is a budget, enforced every frame and proven by the instrument you ship. An AI model in this loop inherits it too.
lines.source: old lab film, line 18 (closing line, kept)
